name: Vitamin E oil / Bio-Oil

lead: Vitamin E oil and cosmetic scar oils such as Bio-Oil are applied to scars and stretch marks in the hope that they will look less obvious. Proponents point to the antioxidant properties of vitamin E and to the moisturizing effect of the oil on the skin.

Vitamin E (tocopherol) is a fat-soluble antioxidant, and the idea is that applying it supports healing and limits scar tissue. Reviews cited by Wikipedia have repeatedly found insufficient evidence for scar-fading claims, and its Scar article says research shows vitamin E to be ineffective for scars.

paras: People massage the oil into the scar or stretch mark once or twice daily, usually for months, often together with scar massage. Products are sold over the counter.
Wikipedia reports vitamin E causes contact dermatitis in up to 33 percent of users and may worsen some scars, though another article notes allergy incidence is low considering widespread use.

angle.text: Vitamin E oil and Bio-Oil are applied to keep scars and stretch marks moisturized, with the aim of making them look less obvious. They are widely used over the counter, and reviews of the evidence have not supported the scar-fading claims.

lead: Vitamin E oil and Bio-Oil are over-the-counter skin oils that people rub onto scars, acne marks and stretch marks in the hope of making them smoother, flatter and less noticeable. Vitamin E is topical tocopherol, a fat-soluble antioxidant sold as pure oil, in puncturable capsules and as an ingredient in creams [1]. Bio-Oil is a branded cosmetic oil blend marketed for scars and stretch marks. For appearance, the appeal is a cheap, easy way to even out skin texture and tone on the face and body, including stretch marks that can appear with rapid muscle or weight gain.

Wikipedia's article on tocopherol notes that topical vitamin E is widely used for wound healing and scar reduction, and that reviews have repeatedly found insufficient evidence for those claims [1]. Its scar article reports that vitamin E has been found ineffective for scars, that it can cause contact dermatitis in up to a third of users and that it may make some scars look worse [2]. The tocopherol article, by contrast, describes allergic reactions to vitamin E derivatives as infrequent given how widely they are used [1].

In lifting and bodybuilding communities, Bio-Oil comes up as a product people try on stretch marks that appear during bulking phases or growth in the legs and arms [3][4][5]. Silicone gels and sheets are the better-studied non-prescription scar products, although a Cochrane analysis summarised on Wikipedia describes the supporting evidence as weak [2].
infobox: Tocopherol (vitamin E) and other oils, depending on product
Pure oil, capsules, blended oils, creams

paras: Topical vitamin E is sold as pure oil, in capsules that people puncture, and as an ingredient in creams and serums. Branded scar oils are typically blends of vegetable oils and vitamins, and Bio-Oil is the best-known example. The scar-oil category is distinct from silicone gels and sheets, which are the most studied non-prescription scar products [2].

Users apply the oils to healed scars from acne, surgery or injury, usually by massaging them in over weeks to months. The stated aim is a flatter, softer and less visible scar. Wikipedia notes that vitamin C and some of its esters, rather than vitamin E, are the topical agents it describes as fading the dark pigment of some scars [2].

Stretch marks form when skin is stretched quickly, as in pregnancy, weight gain or growth spurts, and are linked to rising cortisol levels; bodybuilding and hormone therapy are also listed as contexts [6]. Wikipedia reports a systematic review that found no evidence that topical creams and oils prevent or reduce stretch marks in pregnancy, while tretinoin and hyaluronic acid are described as having reported benefit [6]. Bodybuilders on T Nation describe using Bio-Oil during bulking and for leg growth [3][4][5].

Reviews cited by Wikipedia have repeatedly concluded that there is insufficient evidence that topical vitamin E speeds wound healing or reduces scarring [1]. The scar article states that research has shown vitamin E and onion extract to be ineffective for scars [2]. Silicone gel sheeting has weak supporting evidence from a Cochrane meta-analysis, with the underlying studies described as poor quality [2].

Vitamin E can cause allergic contact dermatitis, with derivatives such as tocopheryl linoleate and tocopherol acetate implicated [1]. The scar article reports contact dermatitis in up to 33 percent of users and that it may worsen some scars [2], while the tocopherol article describes incidence as low relative to how often the vitamin is used [1]. A 2024 case report in an Indian dermatology journal described facial oil granuloma after almond oil and vitamin E oil were injected, which is a different route from topical use [7].

No studies found specific to Bio-Oil are cited here. Studies of topical vitamin E for scars are summarised in reviews that report insufficient evidence [1][2], and a systematic review of creams and oils for pregnancy stretch marks is described in the stretch marks article [6].

Vitamin E and Bio-Oil are mentioned as inexpensive skin-care products for scars and stretch marks. On T Nation, one poster recommended Bio-Oil to another for stretch marks as a product aimed at scars and stretch marks [5], and others mention using it while bulking [3][4].
